policy_title: Require Migrants to Undergo Health Checks and Pay Higher Surcharge/Insurance
stated: The Conservative Party will require migrants to undergo health checks prior to travel and increase their Immigration Health Surcharge or mandate health insurance if they are likely to burden the NHS, and will remove student discounts on the surcharge.

source.quote: We will go further, in line with other countries, by requiring migrants to undergo a health check in advance of travel and increasing their Immigration Health Surcharge or requiring them to buy health insurance if they are likely to be a burden on the NHS. We will increase all visa fees and remove the student discount to the Immigration Health Surcharge to raise more money for public services.

bearing_set.reason: The policy directly affects NHS funding (via increased or restructured Immigration Health Surcharge revenues), NHS demand (pre-travel health screening may redirect high-cost cases), and migrant access to NHS services — all non-negligible effects on healthcare capacity and sustainability.

Conditioning entry and surcharge levels on predicted individual health burden treats migrants with health conditions differently from those without — a genuine equal-treatment/anti-discrimination question bearing on the 'minority protections' and 'equal treatment' indicators under O9.

Mandatory pre-travel health checks constitute state-required bodily examination (bodily autonomy indicator) and compulsory health insurance is a state-imposed financial mandate on individuals — both move the 'freedom from state coercion / mandates' indicator under O10.

Increasing the IHS and removing student discounts raises dedicated NHS levy revenue, directly improving the funded-vs-borrowed balance for NHS expenditure — a concrete mechanism moving the 'is spending funded vs borrowed' indicator under O12.

membership_note: Four fundamentals bear on this policy: the direct NHS capacity and revenue effects (O3), the health-status-based differential treatment of migrants (O9), the bodily-examination and insurance mandates (O10), and the improvement to NHS funding sustainability via higher surcharge receipts (O12). Effects on O13 (labour supply deterrence) are plausible but too speculative at this stage to clear the non-negligible bar without further evidence on volumes and sector mix.
